questions.question: Glass breaks with curved, shell-like fractures while salt crystals cleave into flat faces. What structural difference explains this?
questions.solution: Crystalline solids (salt) have a long-range ORDERED lattice — atoms repeat in a periodic pattern, and cleavage follows the planes of that lattice. Amorphous solids (glass) have only short-range order — no repeating pattern, so fractures follow no planes and are irregular. Long-range order is the discriminator.

questions.question: Name the four bonding types in crystalline solids with one example each, and say which tends to give the highest melting point.
questions.solution: Ionic (NaCl — electrostatic between ions), covalent (diamond — shared electron network), metallic (copper — electron sea around ion cores), molecular/van der Waals (dry ice — weak dipole attraction). Covalent network solids like diamond (and ionic with high charges) give the highest melting points because breaking them means breaking strong directional bonds.

questions.question: Using the energy-band picture, explain why metals conduct, insulators don't, and semiconductors conduct only moderately.
questions.solution: Metals: the valence band is partially filled (or overlaps the conduction band) — electrons find empty states just above and move freely. Insulators: a large forbidden gap (~5+ eV) separates a full valence band from an empty conduction band — thermal energy can't promote electrons. Semiconductors: a SMALL gap (~1 eV) — some electrons cross at room temperature, giving moderate conductivity that rises with temperature (more carriers).

questions.concept: Why semiconductors conduct better when hot
questions.question: Metals conduct worse when heated, but semiconductors conduct better. Explain the opposite behaviours.
questions.solution: In a metal, heating increases lattice vibrations that scatter electrons — mobility falls and resistance rises (carrier count is fixed). In a semiconductor, heating promotes MORE electrons across the small gap — the carrier count grows exponentially and overwhelms the mobility loss. Carrier supply vs carrier scattering decides the sign of the temperature effect.

questions.concept: Doping — a few atoms change everything
questions.question: Why does adding one phosphorus atom per million silicon atoms transform silicon's conductivity?
questions.solution: Phosphorus has 5 valence electrons vs silicon's 4: the extra electron is loosely bound and easily freed into the conduction band — each donor atom contributes one mobile carrier. A millionth of the atoms can multiply the carrier count many-fold, because pure silicon has very few intrinsic carriers. Doping attacks the carrier SUPPLY, which is the bottleneck.
